title: Raw Milk Cheese Microbiomes: A Paradigm for Interactions of Lactic Acid Bacteria in Food Ecosystems
content: While industrial scale dairy fermentations often employ pasteurized milk as the substrate, many farmhouse and traditional production practices apply raw milk derived from a variety of mammals. Certain artisanal production systems rely on the autochthonous microbiota of the milk, fermentation vessels, equipment and/or environment to initiate milk coagulation. While the technological properties of lactic acid bacteria associated with dairy fermentations are well described, their interactions with other organisms during fermentation and cheese ripening are poorly investigated. This study presents an overview of the microbial ecology of raw and pasteurized milk used in the production of cheeses. Furthermore, we report on the motility phenotype, lactose utilization ability and metabolic products of isolates of Hafnia paralvei and Hafnia alvei, and determine that these strains could grow in a non-antagonistic manner on plates with strains of Lactococcus lactis and Streptococcus thermophilus. As artisanal and farmhouse production systems are often associated with protected or regionally significant products, it is essential to develop a clear understanding of the microbial communities within and the complex relationships between the community members.
